source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
# Tomato crop basics

Tomato (`Solanum lycopersicum`) is a warm-season vegetable crop in the Solanaceae family. Greenhouse production is used to reduce exposure to heavy rain, wind and some external pests while allowing better control of irrigation, nutrition, canopy and harvest timing. Protected cultivation does not remove pest or disease risk; it changes the risk profile and makes ventilation, sanitation and monitoring more important.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Main growth stages

A practical farmer-facing sequence is: seed and germination -> nursery seedling -> transplant establishment -> vegetative growth -> first flowering -> fruit set -> fruit enlargement -> colour development -> repeated harvest. Management priorities change by stage. Seedlings need clean media, good drainage and protection from damping-off. After transplanting, root establishment and even moisture are critical. During flowering and fruit set, heat stress, poor pollination and nutrient imbalance can reduce yield. During heavy fruit load, irrigation and nutrient demand rises and irregular moisture can contribute to cracking or blossom-end rot.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Determinate and indeterminate tomatoes

Determinate plants stop extension growth after a limited number of flower clusters and are compact. Indeterminate plants keep extending and are commonly used for long-duration protected cultivation because they can be trained vertically and harvested over many pickings. Indeterminate plants normally require trellising, regular pruning and canopy management.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## What greenhouse cultivation changes

A greenhouse or polyhouse provides a protected growing environment; it is not a gas. The farmer still manages air temperature, humidity, root-zone moisture, light, ventilation, irrigation, fertility and pest exclusion. High performance comes from keeping these factors in balance rather than maximizing one variable.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Farmer questions this article supports

- What is greenhouse tomato cultivation?
- What are tomato growth stages?
- Why are indeterminate tomatoes commonly trained in polyhouses?
- Why does a greenhouse still need pest management?
- At what stage should I focus on irrigation, pollination or fruit quality?

source_name: TNAU Tomato seed and nursery production
text:
# Nursery and transplanting

A healthy crop begins with uniform, disease-free seedlings. Protected nurseries commonly use pro-trays with clean, well-drained growing media and insect-proof protection. One seed per cell makes it easier to maintain uniform plants and reduces root disturbance at transplanting.

source_name: TNAU Tomato seed and nursery production
text:
## Nursery priorities

Use clean trays and media, avoid water stagnation, and provide enough moisture for germination without keeping the media continuously saturated. Overcrowding, poor drainage, high humidity and persistent wetness increase damping-off risk. Inspect seedlings frequently and remove collapsed or suspicious seedlings instead of allowing diseased tissue to remain in the nursery.

A transplant should be sturdy, actively growing and not severely root-bound. Harden seedlings gradually before moving them into the greenhouse so they can adjust to stronger light, air movement and a different watering pattern.

source_name: TNAU Tomato seed and nursery production
text:
## Transplanting

Prepare the bed and irrigation system before transplanting. Moistening the bed before planting helps avoid placing roots into a very dry root zone. Handle the plug carefully so the root ball stays intact. Avoid planting diseased, weak, stretched or mechanically damaged seedlings.

source_name: TNAU Tomato seed and nursery production
text:
## After transplanting

The first objective is root establishment, not rapid fertilizer loading. Keep the root zone evenly moist, check emitter performance and replace failed seedlings early. Watch for wilting that persists despite adequate moisture because it may indicate root disease, stem injury or excessive heat rather than simple water shortage.

source_name: TNAU Tomato seed and nursery production
text:

- How do I raise tomato seedlings?
- Why are my seedlings collapsing?
- When is a seedling ready to transplant?
- Should I use pro-trays?
- What should I check in the first week after transplanting?

topic: Soil, Growing Media, pH and Root Zone
source_name: TNAU Tomato soil and field preparation
text:
# Soil, growing media, pH and root-zone management

Tomato performs best in a well-drained root zone with good aeration and enough organic matter or a well-managed soilless substrate. TNAU describes well-drained loamy soil rich in organic matter as suitable and gives a soil pH range around 6.5–7.5 for field production, while recent ICAR protected-tomato material describes sandy loam around pH 6.0–7.0 as ideal. These ranges overlap around slightly acidic to near-neutral conditions. Local soil and water testing should guide exact correction.

topic: Soil, Growing Media, pH and Root Zone
source_name: TNAU Tomato soil and field preparation
text:
## Why drainage matters

Tomato roots need both water and oxygen. Saturated beds displace air, weaken roots and encourage soil-borne diseases. A farmer should not interpret “soil moisture high” as “better.” The useful target is adequate and stable moisture without prolonged saturation.

topic: Soil, Growing Media, pH and Root Zone
source_name: TNAU Tomato soil and field preparation
text:
## Soil versus soilless media

Soil-grown polyhouses are simpler but can accumulate soil-borne pathogens and salts when poorly managed. Soilless production using media such as cocopeat can improve root-zone control but requires careful irrigation, nutrient solution and drainage management. A media system is not automatically safer; poor sanitation or excessive nutrient concentration can still damage roots.

topic: Soil, Growing Media, pH and Root Zone
source_name: TNAU Tomato soil and field preparation
text:
## pH and nutrient availability

Very acidic or alkaline conditions can make some nutrients less available even when fertilizer is present. If nutrient deficiency symptoms persist despite feeding, check pH, irrigation water quality, drainage and root health rather than repeatedly increasing fertilizer.

topic: Soil, Growing Media, pH and Root Zone
source_name: TNAU Tomato soil and field preparation
text:
## Useful farmer observations

Ask whether water drains quickly, whether the bed smells anaerobic, whether roots are white/cream or brown, whether salt crust is visible, and whether symptoms are uniform across an irrigation line. These clues help distinguish a whole-house nutrient or irrigation issue from an isolated disease problem.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
# Greenhouse and protected cultivation

Protected cultivation uses a structure such as a naturally ventilated polyhouse, shade-net structure or more controlled greenhouse to modify the crop environment. The aim is not to create a perfectly sealed room. The aim is to reduce damaging weather exposure and manage the crop microclimate more consistently.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Common protected structures

Naturally ventilated polyhouses rely mainly on vents and air exchange rather than active cooling. Medium- and high-technology houses may add fans, pads, foggers or automated controls. The most appropriate structure depends on local climate, budget, crop duration and technical support.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Benefits

Potential benefits include off-season production, more consistent quality, efficient drip irrigation and fertigation, vertical training, and lower direct rain exposure. ICAR field demonstrations show that protected tomato can substantially improve productivity and crop duration when the system is managed correctly.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## New risks created by protection

A protected structure can also trap heat or humidity. Insect pests can multiply quickly after entering if monitoring is weak. Reusing contaminated tools or moving through plants when leaves are wet can spread disease. Therefore exclusion, sanitation, ventilation, pruning and regular scouting are core greenhouse practices.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Good farmer mental model

Think of a greenhouse as a system with interacting variables:

- air temperature
- humidity
- light
- ventilation
- root-zone moisture
- irrigation water quality
- nutrition
- plant canopy density
- pest and disease pressure

The “best” condition is the combination that supports healthy growth and fruit set without creating a favourable environment for pests or pathogens.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
# Temperature, humidity and ventilation

Temperature and humidity should be interpreted together. Warm air, strong solar radiation, dense canopy and poor ventilation can create heat stress. High relative humidity with wet foliage and weak air movement can increase disease pressure and reduce effective pollen release. Very dry, hot air can increase transpiration stress and interfere with fruit set.

Recent ICAR protected-tomato material reports that fruit set and colour development perform well around 20–25°C. This is a useful agronomic reference, not a universal hard boundary. Variety, growth stage, night temperature, radiation, ventilation, root-zone moisture and local climate all matter.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Signs that heat is becoming a problem

Plants may wilt during peak radiation despite moist soil, flowers may drop, fruit set may decline, leaves may roll, and the house may remain hot after outside conditions cool. The first response is to inspect ventilation, shading strategy, irrigation timing and canopy density rather than simply adding more fertilizer.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## High humidity problems

Persistent high humidity and leaf wetness can favour several foliar diseases. Dense foliage also reduces air movement. Remove unnecessary lower/diseased leaves, avoid excessive irrigation that raises humidity, ventilate when conditions allow, and keep plants trained so air can move through the canopy.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Greenhouse ML integration

When the ML model predicts `Needs Adjustment` because temperature or humidity contributed strongly, the RAG answer should name the actual XAI factor and recommend checks. Do not invent a threshold that the model did not use. Example: “Humidity is the largest negative factor in your latest analysis. Improve ventilation, check whether irrigation is occurring too late in the day, and inspect for condensation or leaf wetness.”

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
# Light, carbon dioxide and air movement

Tomato is a high-light crop. Light drives photosynthesis, but the farmer must balance light with temperature. In a hot greenhouse, more incoming radiation may push leaf and air temperature beyond the crop’s comfort zone. Shading can reduce heat load, but excessive or unnecessary shading can reduce photosynthesis and fruit production.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Light symptoms

Low-light conditions often produce softer, more elongated growth and can reduce flower and fruit performance. Excess heat combined with strong radiation can cause stress and sunscald. Therefore a greenhouse advisory should not label “light high” or “light low” without considering temperature and growth stage.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## CO2

Carbon dioxide is a gas used by plants during photosynthesis. In a closed or poorly ventilated greenhouse, CO2 can become depleted during active photosynthesis, while ventilation replenishes outside air. Commercial CO2 enrichment is a controlled production technique and should not be recommended casually without appropriate equipment and monitoring.

For the Namma Krushi prototype, CO2 should primarily be treated as a measured environmental feature. If the greenhouse dataset contains CO2, let the trained model learn its relationship with the target and use XAI to explain its contribution. The chatbot should avoid promising yield gains from artificial enrichment unless the farmer has a suitable controlled system.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Air movement

Good air movement helps moderate humidity, reduce condensation and improve canopy uniformity. Excessively stagnant air is undesirable, but strong direct airflow can physically stress plants. Natural ventilation, vents, fans where available, and sensible canopy management should work together.

source_name: ICAR Kharif Agro-Advisories for Farmers 2025
text:
# Irrigation and soil moisture

Tomato needs a dependable water supply, but the root zone should not remain saturated. Drip irrigation is well suited to protected cultivation because it delivers water near the root zone and can be integrated with fertigation.

source_name: ICAR Kharif Agro-Advisories for Farmers 2025
text:
## Avoid the two extremes

Water stress can cause wilting, flower drop, poor fruit enlargement and irregular nutrient uptake. Excess water reduces oxygen around roots and can increase root disease risk. Alternating severe drying with heavy irrigation can contribute to fruit cracking and calcium-related fruit disorders.

source_name: ICAR Kharif Agro-Advisories for Farmers 2025
text:
## Better irrigation decisions

Use soil-moisture measurements as one input, not the only input. Check emitter flow, drainage, crop stage, weather, radiation, substrate type and recent irrigation. The same sensor reading may mean different things in a heavy soil and in a porous cocopeat substrate.

source_name: ICAR Kharif Agro-Advisories for Farmers 2025
text:
## Irrigation timing

Frequent small applications are common in protected systems, especially in soilless media, but the exact schedule must be tuned locally. Avoid routine watering just because a fixed clock says so if the root zone is already wet. A model or rule engine should consider sensor trends and crop stage rather than a single reading.

source_name: ICAR Kharif Agro-Advisories for Farmers 2025
text:
## Diagnostic questions

If plants wilt, ask: Is the media actually dry? Do only plants on one lateral wilt? Is there standing water? Are roots brown? Does the plant recover in evening? Is the greenhouse extremely hot? These answers help separate irrigation failure, heat stress, vascular wilt and root disease.

source_name: TNAU Tomato fertigation
text:
# Fertigation and plant nutrition

Fertigation applies soluble nutrients through irrigation. It can improve precision and labour efficiency, but it also means an irrigation error can become a nutrient error. A blocked emitter can create both water stress and nutrient deficiency in the same plant.

source_name: TNAU Tomato fertigation
text:
## Nutrient roles

Nitrogen supports vegetative growth and chlorophyll. Phosphorus supports roots and energy processes. Potassium is important for water relations, fruit development and quality. Calcium is important for cell-wall integrity and fruit health. Magnesium is part of chlorophyll. Micronutrients such as iron, zinc, boron and manganese are needed in smaller amounts but can still limit growth when unavailable.

source_name: TNAU Tomato fertigation
text:
## Avoid “more fertilizer” thinking

Leaf yellowing is not automatically nitrogen deficiency. Root disease, waterlogging, pH imbalance, salt accumulation, magnesium or iron issues, old-leaf senescence and viral disease can all produce yellowing. A chatbot should ask where symptoms begin, whether veins remain green, whether roots are healthy, and whether the problem is uniform.

source_name: TNAU Tomato fertigation
text:
## Fertigation monitoring

Useful checks include irrigation-water quality, pH, electrical conductivity where equipment is available, injector calibration, stock-solution mixing, emitter uniformity and drainage. A sudden whole-house symptom after a fertigation event suggests a system-level issue and deserves immediate inspection.

source_name: TNAU Tomato fertigation
text:
## Greenhouse advisory behavior

When XAI identifies a sensor parameter, the chatbot should not infer a nutrient deficiency unless the model actually includes nutrition data or the user reports diagnostic symptoms. Environmental ML and nutrient diagnosis are related but not interchangeable.

source_name: Two-stem training in polyhouse tomato
text:
# Training, pruning and trellising

Indeterminate greenhouse tomatoes are normally supported vertically so the canopy remains accessible for scouting, harvesting and air movement. ICAR and TNAU materials describe staking or rope training and regular removal of unwanted side shoots.

source_name: Two-stem training in polyhouse tomato
text:
## Why train plants

Training keeps foliage and fruit away from the ground, improves light distribution, creates working space and supports a long crop cycle. It also helps spray coverage when plant-protection treatments are genuinely needed.

source_name: Two-stem training in polyhouse tomato
text:
## Pruning principles

Remove unwanted side shoots while they are small. Avoid severe pruning that suddenly exposes fruit to intense sunlight. Use clean hands or tools and avoid moving disease from plant to plant. Remove lower leaves gradually when they are old, diseased, touching the soil or seriously restricting airflow.

ICAR-IIVR has demonstrated a two-stem system for indeterminate tomato in a polyhouse: the main stem plus one selected side shoot are retained. This is one production option, not a universal rule; spacing, cultivar and support structure should match the chosen training system.

source_name: Two-stem training in polyhouse tomato
text:
## Disease connection

Dense, unmanaged canopies trap humidity and make scouting difficult. However, excessive pruning can stress plants and reduce photosynthetic area. The target is a balanced canopy with good air movement and adequate leaf area.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
# Pollination, flowering and fruit set

Tomato flowers are self-pollinating, but pollen still needs to be released effectively. In protected cultivation, low air movement, cloudy weather, very high humidity, heat stress or poor plant balance can reduce fruit set.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Practical pollination support

Recent ICAR protected-tomato guidance notes that manual shaking, air movement or electric vibration can support pollination under cloudy or foggy conditions. The goal is gentle vibration of flower clusters, not physical damage.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Why flowers drop

Blossom drop can result from excessive heat, temperature extremes, water stress, very high humidity, poor pollination, heavy vegetative growth, nutrient imbalance, root stress or pest/disease injury. It is therefore a symptom category rather than one diagnosis.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Chatbot diagnostic sequence

Ask about greenhouse temperature during flowering, whether flowers are shedding before fruit formation, whether pollen appears powdery or sticky, whether plants are wilted, whether recent irrigation has been irregular, and whether the crop has excessive vegetative growth. Then retrieve the relevant environment, irrigation or nutrition article.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Fruit set versus fruit enlargement

A flower can set fruit successfully and still abort later if the plant is under stress. Once fruit set occurs, steady irrigation and balanced nutrition become increasingly important as fruit load rises.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
# Harvest and postharvest

Harvest stage depends on market distance and intended use. Recent ICAR protected-tomato material distinguishes mature-green harvest for longer transport, pink-stage harvest for shorter movement, and fully red fruit for immediate consumption or processing. Local market preference should decide the practical stage.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Harvest hygiene

Pick regularly, handle fruit gently, avoid dropping or compressing fruit, and use clean harvest containers. Remove damaged or diseased fruit from the production area rather than leaving it as a pest or pathogen source.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Quality factors

Uniform colour, firmness, freedom from cracking, absence of blossom-end rot, pest injury and sunscald all affect market value. Many quality problems begin before harvest, so postharvest handling cannot correct poor irrigation or nutrition during fruit development.

source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## History data in Namma Krushi

The application can store disease detections and greenhouse analyses over time. A farmer may then ask whether fruit-quality problems started after a period of heat, humidity or irrigation stress. The chatbot should use stored history only when that context is actually provided by the application.

source_name: TNAU Tomato calcium deficiency and blossom end rot
text:
# Physiological disorders

Physiological disorders are non-infectious problems caused by the interaction of water, nutrients, temperature, light and plant growth. They may resemble disease but are not necessarily caused by a pathogen.

source_name: TNAU Tomato calcium deficiency and blossom end rot
text:
## Blossom-end rot

Blossom-end rot appears as a sunken dark lesion at the blossom end of fruit and is strongly associated with inadequate calcium reaching developing fruit. This can happen even when soil calcium is present because irregular water supply, root stress or rapid growth disrupts calcium transport. Stabilize irrigation and investigate root-zone conditions before assuming that simply adding calcium will solve the problem.

source_name: TNAU Tomato calcium deficiency and blossom end rot
text:
## Fruit cracking

Cracking is commonly associated with sudden changes in water availability and rapid fruit expansion. Keeping soil moisture more uniform and avoiding severe dry-wet cycles helps reduce risk. Variety and weather also influence susceptibility.

source_name: TNAU Tomato calcium deficiency and blossom end rot
text:
## Sunscald

Fruit exposed suddenly to intense sunlight after heavy pruning or leaf loss can develop pale or damaged areas. Maintain adequate foliage around fruit while still managing canopy airflow.

source_name: TNAU Tomato calcium deficiency and blossom end rot
text:
## Puffiness and poor filling

Poor pollination, nutrition imbalance and environmental stress can produce fruit with poor internal filling. Check flowering conditions and overall plant balance.

source_name: TNAU Tomato calcium deficiency and blossom end rot
text:
## Important distinction

If a lesion spreads between plants, produces characteristic leaf spots, vascular browning, fungal growth, bacterial ooze or is associated with insect vectors, consider an infectious disease rather than a purely physiological disorder.

text:
# Healthy tomato leaf

A healthy tomato leaf is typically green, turgid and free from expanding lesions, unusual mosaic patterns, heavy curling, bronzing, webbing or widespread necrosis. Minor old-leaf yellowing, dust, mechanical tears, nutrient variation or insect feeding can occur without representing a major disease.

A CNN prediction of `Healthy` should still be treated as an image classification result, not proof that the entire plant is healthy. The image may not show roots, stems, fruit, lower canopy, mites on the underside of leaves or early symptoms outside the photographed area.

If the farmer reports serious symptoms despite a healthy image classification, ask for another image and symptom description rather than dismissing the concern.

source_name: TNAU Bacterial leaf spot of tomato
text:
# Bacterial spot

Bacterial spot can produce small water-soaked lesions that darken and may develop a yellow halo. Fruit can develop small raised or scabby lesions. Moist weather, persistent dew and splash help spread bacterial inoculum.

source_name: TNAU Bacterial leaf spot of tomato
text:
## Distinguishing clues

Look for many small lesions rather than large concentric-ring lesions typical of early blight. Ask whether fruit also has rough spots and whether the greenhouse recently had prolonged leaf wetness or splash.

source_name: TNAU Bacterial leaf spot of tomato
text:
## Management principles

Start with disease-free seed/seedlings, sanitation, removal of badly affected tissue where practical, reduction of splash, and disinfection of tools. Avoid working through wet plants. Because bactericides and pesticide registrations vary, chemical treatment should follow current local guidance rather than a hard-coded chatbot dose.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
# Early blight

Early blight is associated with `Alternaria` and commonly produces brown to dark lesions that enlarge with concentric rings, giving a target or bull's-eye appearance. Symptoms often begin on older leaves and can be accompanied by yellowing around lesions. Stem and fruit lesions can also occur.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Favouring conditions

Warm conditions, leaf wetness, high humidity and infected plant debris can increase disease pressure. Dense canopies that stay damp are a management concern.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Management principles

Remove heavily infected debris, improve airflow, avoid unnecessary leaf wetness, maintain balanced crop nutrition and rotate where possible. Use disease-free planting material. If fungicide intervention is required, use a currently registered product and local extension recommendation.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
# Late blight

Late blight can progress rapidly under cool-to-mild, wet and humid conditions. Leaves develop expanding dark or water-soaked lesions, and stems and fruit can also be affected. Under very humid conditions, pale fungal growth may be visible near lesion margins, especially on the lower leaf surface.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Why it matters

Rapid progression distinguishes late blight from many slower leaf spots. A farmer reporting a sudden whole-house increase in dark lesions after prolonged humidity or wet foliage should treat the situation as urgent.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Management principles

Remove infected tissue when feasible, reduce prolonged leaf wetness, improve ventilation, avoid overhead wetting and follow an integrated disease-management program. Confirm locally before chemical treatment because product approvals and resistance-management recommendations change.

text:
# Leaf mold

Leaf mold is especially associated with protected cultivation and humid, poorly ventilated canopies. Typical symptoms include pale or yellow patches on the upper leaf surface with olive-green to brown fungal growth on the corresponding lower surface. Older leaves are often affected first.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Distinguishing clues

The visible fungal growth on the underside and a high-humidity greenhouse history are important clues. It can be confused with nutrient yellowing if the underside is not checked.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Management principles

Improve ventilation, reduce persistent humidity, avoid dense foliage, remove badly infected leaves and keep plant spacing/training adequate for air movement. Resistant cultivars can be valuable where the disease is recurrent.

source_name: TNAU Septoria leaf spot of tomato
text:
# Septoria leaf spot

Septoria produces many small round-to-irregular leaf spots, often with a greyish centre and darker margin. Spots can merge, causing blighting and defoliation. High humidity and infected crop debris contribute to disease development and spread.

source_name: TNAU Septoria leaf spot of tomato
text:
## Distinguishing clues

Compared with early blight, Septoria spots are generally smaller and do not show the same prominent concentric-ring pattern. Heavy defoliation can expose fruit to sunscald.

source_name: TNAU Septoria leaf spot of tomato
text:
## Management principles

Remove infected debris, reduce splash and prolonged leaf wetness, improve ventilation, and maintain sanitation. Use current local recommendations if a fungicide is required.

topic: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl / Leaf Curl Virus
source_name: TNAU Tomato leaf curl
text:
# Tomato yellow leaf curl / leaf curl virus

Leaf curl disease is associated with severe curling or crinkling of leaves, shortened internodes, stunting and a bushy appearance. Whiteflies are important vectors for tomato leaf-curl viruses.

topic: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl / Leaf Curl Virus
source_name: TNAU Tomato leaf curl
text:
## Distinguishing clues

A plant can curl leaves from heat or water stress, so look for persistent distorted new growth, stunting and whitefly presence. Virus-infected plants do not recover simply by correcting irrigation.

topic: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl / Leaf Curl Virus
source_name: TNAU Tomato leaf curl
text:
## Management principles

Begin with healthy seedlings, use insect-exclusion practices, monitor whiteflies with sticky traps, remove strongly infected plants early when appropriate, control weed hosts and manage whitefly populations with an IPM program. Virus management focuses heavily on prevention because there is no curative spray that removes virus from an infected plant.

source_name: TNAU Mosaic disease of tomato
text:
# Tomato mosaic virus / mosaic disease

Mosaic disease causes irregular light- and dark-green mottling, distortion, puckering and sometimes narrow or fern-like leaflets. Plants may be stunted. Some mosaic viruses can spread mechanically through hands, tools, contaminated debris or planting material.

source_name: TNAU Mosaic disease of tomato
text:
## Distinguishing clues

Mosaic is a pattern across leaf tissue rather than discrete fungal spots. Nutrient deficiency may cause chlorosis but usually follows vein or leaf-age patterns rather than a patchy mosaic.

source_name: TNAU Mosaic disease of tomato
text:
## Management principles

Use disease-free seed and seedlings, remove clearly infected plants when recommended, sanitize tools and hands, avoid unnecessary handling, manage weeds and crop residues, and follow hygiene between greenhouse sections.

source_name: TNAU Powdery mildew of tomato
text:
# Powdery mildew

Powdery mildew can cause yellowish leaf areas and visible white powdery fungal growth. Unlike diseases that require free water on leaves, powdery mildew can develop under relatively dry leaf surfaces when the greenhouse climate otherwise favours the pathogen.

source_name: TNAU Powdery mildew of tomato
text:
## Distinguishing clues

Look for superficial white growth that can spread across affected areas. Do not confuse mineral deposits from irrigation water with fungal growth; inspect multiple leaves and both surfaces.

source_name: TNAU Powdery mildew of tomato
text:
## Management principles

Improve sanitation and airflow, remove heavily affected tissue, avoid excessive canopy density and use resistant material when available. If chemical control is required, rotate modes of action according to current local guidance to reduce resistance risk.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
# Target spot

“Target spot” is used for circular leaf lesions with concentric zoning caused by certain fungal pathogens. Image datasets may use this as a separate class from early blight even though both can show target-like rings.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Diagnostic caution

Because visual overlap is strong, a CNN prediction of `Target Spot` should be described as a likely class rather than a laboratory-confirmed diagnosis. Ask whether lesions occur on older foliage, whether fruit/stems are affected, and how quickly the problem is spreading.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Management principles

Sanitation, removal of heavily infected debris, airflow, avoidance of prolonged leaf wetness and appropriate crop-protection guidance are sensible general measures. For exact pathogen confirmation or chemical choice, consult local plant pathology or horticulture services.

source_name: TNAU Red spider mite on tomato
text:
# Spider mites / two-spotted spider mite

Spider mites are pests, not fungal diseases. Feeding causes stippling, bronzing or reddish-brown foliage. With heavier infestation, fine webbing may be visible and leaves can dry. Flower and fruit formation can be affected when populations become high.

source_name: TNAU Red spider mite on tomato
text:
## Distinguishing clues

Inspect the underside of leaves with a magnifier. Tiny moving mites, eggs and fine webbing strongly support a mite diagnosis. Heat and dry conditions often favour rapid mite multiplication.

source_name: TNAU Red spider mite on tomato
text:
## Management principles

Scout early, remove severely infested leaves where practical, reduce plant stress, avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticide use that destroys natural enemies, and use locally recommended biological or acaricide options when thresholds justify treatment.

source_name: TNAU Damping off of tomato
text:
# Damping off

Damping off is mainly a nursery problem. Seeds or seedlings may rot before emergence, while emerged seedlings develop soft water-soaked tissue near the base and collapse. Wet, crowded, poorly drained nursery conditions strongly favour the problem.

source_name: TNAU Damping off of tomato
text:
## Management principles

Use clean trays and media, avoid overwatering, provide drainage and airflow, remove collapsed seedlings, reduce overcrowding and use healthy treated seed according to local nursery recommendations. Once seedlings have collapsed, restoring them is usually not possible; prevention is the main strategy.

source_name: TNAU Fusarium wilt of tomato
text:
# Fusarium wilt

Fusarium wilt commonly begins with yellowing of lower leaves followed by drooping and progressive wilt. Browning of the vascular tissue inside the stem is an important diagnostic clue. The pathogen survives in soil and can spread through contaminated debris, water and equipment.

source_name: TNAU Fusarium wilt of tomato
text:
## Distinguishing clues

Cut a symptomatic lower stem lengthwise. Brown vascular tissue supports a vascular-wilt diagnosis, whereas simple heat stress usually does not produce vascular browning. Wilt may initially affect one side of a plant.

source_name: TNAU Fusarium wilt of tomato
text:
## Management principles

Use resistant cultivars where available, start with healthy seedlings, rotate with non-hosts, remove infected plants, sanitize tools and manage contaminated soil/media. Avoid moving soil between clean and affected greenhouse zones.

source_name: TNAU Bacterial wilt of tomato
text:
# Bacterial wilt

Bacterial wilt can cause rapid wilt of an otherwise green plant, sometimes with lower-leaf drooping first. Cut stems may show vascular discoloration and bacterial ooze. High soil moisture can favour disease development.

source_name: TNAU Bacterial wilt of tomato
text:
## Distinguishing clues

Sudden permanent wilt despite adequate water, plus vascular symptoms, is more concerning than temporary midday wilt that recovers in evening. Bacterial wilt can persist in infested soil and spread through contaminated water, soil, tools and planting material.

source_name: TNAU Bacterial wilt of tomato
text:
## Management principles

Use disease-free seedlings, remove infected plants and contaminated root material, sanitize tools, improve drainage, avoid moving infested soil, and rotate where possible. Local resistant rootstocks or cultivars may be part of a long-term strategy.

text:
# Tomato spotted wilt

Tomato spotted wilt virus can cause bronzing, spotting, leaf distortion, stunting and ring-like symptoms on fruit. Thrips are important vectors.

source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Management principles

Use clean planting material, exclude and monitor thrips, remove infected plants when appropriate, manage weeds that can host both virus and thrips, and maintain greenhouse sanitation. Because the virus cannot be cured inside an infected plant, vector management and prevention are central.

source_name: TNAU Fusarium wilt of tomato
text:
# Yellow leaves: diagnostic guide

“Leaves are yellow” is not a diagnosis. Ask four questions first:

1. Are older/lower leaves affected first, or new leaves?
2. Is yellowing uniform, between veins, around spots, or mixed with mosaic?
3. Are roots healthy and the soil well drained?
4. Are there pests, webbing, leaf curl, wilting or visible lesions?

source_name: TNAU Fusarium wilt of tomato
text:
## Common possibilities

Older-leaf yellowing can occur with normal senescence, nitrogen/magnesium problems, root stress, Fusarium wilt or foliar disease. New-leaf distortion and yellowing with severe curling suggests a virus/vector problem. Yellow halos around spots point toward a leaf-spot disease. Interveinal yellowing may suggest a nutrient-availability issue. Whole-plant pale growth after waterlogging may indicate root-zone dysfunction.

The chatbot should not jump directly to fertilizer. Retrieve the disease, irrigation, root-zone or nutrition article that matches the observed pattern.

source_name: TNAU Fusarium wilt of tomato
text:
# Wilting: diagnostic guide

First determine whether the plant recovers after the hottest part of the day. Temporary midday wilt with moist soil can be heat/transpiration stress. Persistent wilt needs deeper investigation.

source_name: TNAU Fusarium wilt of tomato
text:
## Check in this order

- Is the root zone dry, waterlogged or normal?
- Is the drip emitter working?
- Is only one irrigation line affected?
- Are roots brown or decayed?
- Does the cut stem show vascular browning or bacterial ooze?
- Are lower leaves yellowing first?
- Is greenhouse temperature extreme?

Persistent wilt despite adequate water can indicate Fusarium wilt, bacterial wilt, root damage or severe stem injury. Avoid automatically adding more water to already saturated soil.

# Flower drop and poor fruit set

Possible causes include heat stress, temperature extremes, high humidity, poor pollen release, water stress, excessive vegetative growth, nutrient imbalance, thrips injury and disease.

topic: Flower Drop and Poor Fruit Set
source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Practical checks

Look at temperature during flowering, ventilation, recent irrigation consistency, pollen release, canopy density and pest presence in flowers. In cloudy or foggy protected conditions, gentle flower-cluster vibration may support pollination. If the problem is concentrated during a hot period, prioritize heat and ventilation management before changing fertilizer.

topic: How to Convert Greenhouse ML + XAI into Farmer Advice
source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
# Converting greenhouse ML and XAI into advice

The greenhouse model should produce a prediction such as `Suitable`, `Needs Adjustment`, or `Unsuitable`, together with probability/confidence and an XAI explanation. The RAG layer then turns the important factors into agronomic advice.

topic: How to Convert Greenhouse ML + XAI into Farmer Advice
source_name: ICAR Indian Horticulture May–June 2026: protected/polyhouse tomato material
text:
## Example

Model output:
- Prediction: Needs Adjustment
- Probability: 0.84
- XAI: humidity contributed negatively; light intensity contributed negatively; temperature was acceptable.

RAG behavior:
1. Retrieve the humidity/ventilation article.
2. Retrieve the light article.
3. Tell the farmer what is already acceptable.
4. Recommend practical checks such as ventilation, condensation, irrigation timing, shading or light obstruction.
5. Do not claim the model measured a nutrient deficiency or disease unless those inputs exist.

topic: How to Convert Greenhouse ML + XAI into Farmer Advice

text:

Store the latest greenhouse result in SQLite. When the farmer asks “Why is my greenhouse not suitable?” pass the actual latest prediction and XAI factors into the chatbot context before retrieval.

# Converting image classification into advice

A disease classifier should return the class and confidence. The chatbot should retrieve the matching disease article and explain what the class means, what symptoms to check, and the first-line management steps.

topic: How to Convert CNN Disease Prediction into Farmer Advice
source_name: TNAU Tomato major and minor diseases index
text:
## Confidence-aware wording

High confidence: “The image most closely matches Early Blight.”
Moderate confidence: “The model suggests Early Blight, but visual overlap exists with other leaf spots.”
Low confidence: “The image is not clear enough for a reliable diagnosis. Please upload another image showing the whole leaf and a close-up.”

Never present a model label as laboratory confirmation. If symptoms conflict with the predicted class, ask for another image or local expert inspection.

source_name: Integrated Pest Management approaches against major insect pests and diseases of Tomato
text:
# Whiteflies

Whiteflies feed on leaf sap and can produce honeydew that supports sooty mould. More importantly in tomato, whiteflies transmit important leaf-curl viruses. Protected environments can allow populations to build quickly after entry.

source_name: Integrated Pest Management approaches against major insect pests and diseases of Tomato
text:
## Monitoring and prevention

Use insect-proof nursery protection, inspect new seedlings, remove weed hosts, use yellow sticky traps for monitoring and keep greenhouse openings/exclusion systems in good condition. Inspect leaf undersides because immature stages are easy to miss.

source_name: Integrated Pest Management approaches against major insect pests and diseases of Tomato
text:
## Management principle

Treat whitefly as both a direct pest and a virus vector. A low visible population can still matter when virus is present in the area. Use integrated management and current local recommendations rather than repeated unscheduled insecticide spraying.

source_name: TNAU Thrips on tomato
text:
# Thrips

Thrips scrape plant tissue and can cause silvery streaking, bud damage and premature flower drop. They are also vectors of tomato spotted wilt virus.

source_name: TNAU Thrips on tomato
text:
## Monitoring

Inspect flowers and tender leaves, use appropriate sticky traps, and watch for silvery feeding scars. Because thrips can hide in flowers, leaf-only inspection may underestimate the population.

source_name: TNAU Thrips on tomato
text:
## Management

Keep weeds under control, use exclusion where practical, remove heavily infested material, conserve beneficial insects and use local IPM guidance for treatment decisions.

# Serpentine leaf miner

Leaf-miner larvae tunnel within leaves, producing winding or serpentine mines. Heavy injury reduces useful leaf area and can lead to drying and premature leaf drop.

text:
# Tomato fruit borer

Fruit-borer caterpillars feed on foliage when young and later bore into developing fruit, creating holes and secondary rot. One larva can damage multiple fruits.

source_name: Integrated Pest Management approaches against major insect pests and diseases of Tomato
text:
## Integrated management

Remove damaged fruit and visible larvae, monitor adult moths with pheromone traps, use trap-crop strategies such as marigold where locally recommended, support natural enemies and use need-based treatment rather than calendar spraying. ICAR-NRIIPM tomato IPM material emphasizes combining multiple tactics.

source_name: Integrated Pest Management approaches against major insect pests and diseases of Tomato
text:
# Integrated pest management (IPM)

IPM combines prevention, monitoring and multiple compatible control methods. The objective is not “zero insects at all times”; it is to prevent economically damaging populations and disease-vector pressure while avoiding unnecessary pesticide use.

source_name: Integrated Pest Management approaches against major insect pests and diseases of Tomato
text:
## Core components

1. Start with healthy seedlings and clean growing media.
2. Use insect-proof nursery protection and maintain greenhouse exclusion.
3. Keep weeds and crop residues under control.
4. Train plants so the canopy can be inspected.
5. Use sticky traps and pheromone traps for monitoring appropriate pests.
6. Use trap crops or barrier crops where locally validated.
7. Conserve or release beneficial organisms when part of the local program.
8. Remove severely infested or infected plant material.
9. Use pesticides only when justified and follow current registration, label, waiting period and resistance-management advice.

The chatbot should ask which pest is present and what evidence supports it before recommending an intervention.
